source.title: Sparse but not Simpler: A Multi-Level Interpretability Analysis of Vision Transformers

record.file_problem: none noted; the full paper, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether increasing weight sparsity improves neuron-level interpretability in a supervised vision transformer and reports that neuron-level proxies remain largely unchanged. This is a refinement of the claim’s neuron-interpretability argument, though it does not reproduce the Qwen audit.
record.gate_note: The neuron results in Sec. 4.2 are relevant to V4’s neuron-interpretability aspect. The study does not estimate the share of interpretable neurons or compare architectures or explanation tools. SAE, circuit, and attribution results are not rows because they do not measure the neuron-level share named by the tested version. The pruning accuracy results are setup, not interpretability outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study asks whether post-hoc Wanda pruning makes DeiT-III B/16 neurons more class-selective. No version makes that claim. V4 says interpretable-neuron shares rise with better explanation tools and modern architectures. It says nothing about pruning a fixed architecture. The measures (AUROC class selectivity, label entropy over 1,000 classes, within-class coefficient of variation, top-50 ablation impact) are class-level proxies, not a share of neurons with one main job. A neuron with a coherent sub-class feature would still show high class entropy. So this is a related but different construct, recorded under fits_no_version. The paper does not cite or use the essay or the OpenAI scoring work.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that weight sparsity shrinks circuit edge counts (about 2.5× fewer at 70%) but does not systematically improve neuron selectivity, SAE feature interpretability or attribution faithfulness. They report that sparse circuits recruit more nodes ('representation spreading'). They note limits: post-hoc pruning only, proxy metrics, supervised ImageNet ViTs only.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares dense and Wanda-pruned DeiT-III B/16 vision models using neuron metrics, SAEs, circuit masks, and attribution faithfulness. It does not perform the Qwen neuron-pole audit or test explanations against held-out activating examples.
record.method_sensitivity: Neuron ablation impact varies somewhat by layer: a narrow high-score tail appears in early and middle layers at 70% sparsity, while block 11 shows only a small increase in sparse-model sensitivity. The paper reports no consistent sparsity-related changes in selectivity, class variance, or label entropy.

fits_no_version.finding: In DeiT-III B/16, Wanda pruning to 10–70% sparsity (with fine-tuning) leaves neuron class selectivity, label entropy and class variance essentially unchanged in blocks 2, 7 and 11. Ablation impact rises only in a narrow tail at 70% sparsity. The authors say neurons remain 'similarly polysemantic' by class-level proxies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-hoc weight pruning does not make vision-transformer neurons more class-selective or less class-polysemantic.

record.problems: The neuron-level outcomes are reported qualitatively in the text and figure, without numerical metric values or uncertainty estimates. The analysis uses proxy measures rather than ground-truth concept annotations and concerns one supervised vision architecture with post-hoc pruning.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. SAE-feature, circuit, and attribution outcomes were left out because they do not measure the neuron-level share named by V4.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or job-share estimates.
No language models, MoE models or scale comparison.
No InceptionV1 cat/car analysis and no test of recursive generalization versus superposition.
No comparison of explanation tools or of architectures, and no interpretable-neuron share. Pruning one fixed ViT is not the architecture or tool change V4 names.
No neuron-based attribution graphs for a large model; the circuits are learned node masks on a ViT, with no comparison against a replacement model.
No test of activating-example explanations on held-out activations.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T5' with a V4 limits_scope label is rejected. V4 attributes messy neurons to architecture, regularization and weak tools, and predicts gains from better tools and modern architectures. It does not predict that pruning a fixed model helps, and the study measures class-level proxies rather than interpretable-neuron shares. The study asserts but does not test that supervised ViT neurons are highly polysemantic; that is a background assumption contrary to the essay. All neuron results are qualitative, from violin plots, with no numbers in the text.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit or estimate of the proportions of neuron poles with one job, two related jobs, or unknown jobs.
No cross-model or scale comparison, and no language models or mixture-of-experts models.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car analysis or test of recursive generalization versus superposition.

The study tests neuron-interpretability proxies under Wanda pruning in one fixed vision architecture. It does not compare explanation tools or architectures, estimate a share of interpretable neurons, or test the stated InceptionV1-sized model estimates.
No attribution graphs built from a large model’s own neurons and no comparison with a trained replacement model or its reconstruction error.
No explanation-from-activating-examples test of predictions on examples the explanation was not written from.
No automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.

rows.subject: DeiT-III B/16
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean ablation impact for top-50 neurons selected per category after Wanda pruning.
rows.measure: Neuron mean ablation impact; top-50 neurons per category across 1,000 ImageNet categories.
rows.baseline: Dense model; numerical baseline not stated.
rows.value: At 70% sparsity, a small number of categories have unusually high mean ablation scores; this is a narrow tail and does not generalize.
rows.note: The text describes a limited effect at 70% sparsity, not a general shift in the distribution; exact values are not given.
rows.check: Measures how pruning changes top-50 ablation impact, not V4's share of interpretable neurons. The high-score tail appears only at 70% sparsity in blocks 2 and 7. Fig. 2 compares sparsity levels 0.1–0.7, and the text does not say a dense distribution is plotted, so 'Dense model' as baseline is unverified.

rows.subject: DeiT-III B/16
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean ablation impact for top-50 neurons selected per category after Wanda pruning.
rows.measure: Neuron mean ablation impact; top-50 neurons per category across 1,000 ImageNet categories.
rows.baseline: Dense model; numerical baseline not stated.
rows.value: Both dense and sparse models have occasional high-ablation outliers; the sparse model is slightly more sensitive in block 11, but the difference is small and does not systematically correlate with increasing sparsity.
rows.note: The reported difference is small and inconsistent across sparsity levels; exact values are not given.
rows.check: The authors call the block-11 difference small and not correlated with sparsity, which fits absent rather than partial. Not V4's construct. The dense comparison is only stated qualitatively.

rows.subject: DeiT-III B/16
rows.operation_detail: Measured neuron class selectivity after Wanda pruning.
rows.measure: Neuron selectivity, computed as AUROC for CLS-token activation against class labels.
rows.baseline: Dense model; numerical baseline not stated.
rows.value: No consistent changes in selectivity across the majority of categories.
rows.note: The paper reports the qualitative result across sparsity levels and layers; values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Class-selectivity AUROC is a class-level proxy, not the share of neurons with one main job. Methods say metrics are averaged over 100 categories, but results and Fig. 2 say 1,000; the category count is inconsistent.

rows.subject: DeiT-III B/16
rows.operation_detail: Measured class variance of neuron responses after Wanda pruning.
rows.measure: Class variance, computed as the coefficient of variation of per-image maximum patch activations.
rows.baseline: Dense model; numerical baseline not stated.
rows.value: Class variance remains stable across sparsity levels.
rows.note: The paper reports the qualitative result across sparsity levels and layers; values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Within-class variability proxy; does not measure V4's construct.

rows.subject: DeiT-III B/16
rows.operation_detail: Measured neuron label entropy after Wanda pruning.
rows.measure: Label entropy over each neuron’s class activation distribution.
rows.baseline: Dense model; numerical baseline not stated.
rows.value: Label entropy remains high across sparsity levels; no consistent changes are observed across the majority of categories.
rows.note: The paper interprets high entropy as neurons remaining similarly polysemantic; numerical values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Label entropy over ImageNet classes. High entropy does not show polysemanticity in the essay's sense, since a neuron can track a coherent sub-class feature. Not V4's construct.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Wanda-pruned DeiT-III B/16 at sparsity levels 0.1–0.7
reader_labels.reason: Neuron-level proxies show no consistent improvement with pruning; late-layer ablation sensitivity rises only slightly, while selectivity, class variance, and label entropy do not systematically improve (r1–r5). This tests pruning in one fixed architecture, not the version’s claims about better tools or architecture comparisons.
